subdue.e: From Middle English subdewen, subduen, sodewen, from Old French souduire, from Latin subdūcō (“to draw away”), perhaps influenced by subdō (“to subdue, subject”).
subdue.g: To overcome, quieten, or bring under control.

subject.e: From Middle English subget, from Old French suget, from Latin subiectus (“lying under or near, adjacent, also subject, exposed”), as a noun, subiectus (“a subject, an inferior”), subiectum (“the subject of a proposition”), past participle of subiciō (“throw, lay, place”).
subject.g: Likely to be affected by or to experience something; liable.

subject.e: From Latin subiectus (“a subject, an inferior”), subiectum (“the subject of a proposition”), past participle of subiciō (“throw, lay, place”), from sub (“under, at the foot of”) + iaciō (“throw, hurl”).
subject.g: The noun, pronoun or noun phrase about whom the statement is made. In active clauses with verbs denoting an action, the subject is the actor

subjection.e: From Middle English subjectioun, from Anglo-Norman subjectioun, Old French subjection (Modern French sujétion), and their etymon Latin subjectiō. By surface analysis, subject + -ion.
subjection.g: The act of bringing something under the control of something else.

submerge.e: Borrowed from Latin submergere, from sub (“under”) + mergere (“to plunge”). By surface analysis, sub- + merge.

submission.e: From Middle English submissioun, from Old French soubmission, from Latin submissio, from submitto.
submission.g: The act of submitting or yielding; surrender.

submit.e: From Middle English submitten, borrowed from Latin submittere, infinitive of submittō (“place under, yield”), from sub (“under, from below, up”) + mitto (“to send”).
submit.g: To yield or give way to another.

suborn.e: PIE word upó Borrowed from Anglo-Norman suburner, subhorner, and Middle French suborner, subourner (“to induce (someone) to commit a crime (specifically perjury) or wrongdoing”) (modern French suborner (“to suborn; to bribe”)), and from its etymon Latin subōrnāre, the present active infinitive of subōrnō (“to incite, instigate, suborn.
suborn.g: To induce (someone) to commit an unlawful or malicious act, especially in a corrupt manner.

subscribe.e: From Middle English subscriben, subskryben, from Latin subscrībere (“write beneath”). By surface analysis, sub- + scribe.
subscribe.g: To write (one’s name) at the bottom of a document; to sign (one's name).

subsequent.e: Borrowed from Middle French subséquent, from Latin subsequentis, form of subsequēns, present participle of subsequor (“to follow, to succeed”).
subsequent.g: Following in time; coming or being after something else at any time, indefinitely.

subside.g: To sink or fall to the bottom; to settle, as lees.

substance.e: From Middle English substance, from Old French substance, from Latin substantia (“substance, essence”), from substāns, present active participle of substō (“exist”, literally “stand under”), from sub + stō (“stand”).

substantial.e: From Middle English substancial, substantiall, from Old French substanciel, substantiel and its etymon Latin substantiālis.

substitute.e: From Middle English substituten, from Latin substitutus, past participle of substituō, from sub- (“under; beneath”) + statuō (“to put up; establish”).
substitute.g: To use in place of something else, with the same function.

substitution.e: From Middle French substitution, from Late Latin substitutio.
substitution.g: The act of substituting or the state of being substituted.

subtract.e: Borrowed from Latin subtractus, perfect passive participle of subtrahō (“to draw from beneath; withdraw, remove”); from sub (“under”) + trahō (“to draw, pull, drag”).
subtract.g: To remove or reduce; especially to reduce a quantity or number.

suburb.e: From Old French suburbe, subburbe, from Latin suburbium (from sub- (“under-”) + urbs (“city”)).
suburb.g: A residential area located on the outskirts of a city or large town that usually includes businesses that cater to its residents; such as sc

subvert.e: From Middle English subverten, from Old French subvertir, from Latin subvertō (“to overthrow”, literally “to underturn, turn from beneath”).
subvert.g: To overturn from the foundation; to overthrow; to ruin utterly.

subvert.e: Back-formation from subvertising, by analogy with advert.

succeed.e: From Old French succeder, from Latin succedere (“to go under, go from under, come under, approach, follow, take the place of, receive by succession, prosper, be successful”). Partly displaced English speed, of which the original sense “to succeed” only survives in a few fossilized expressions such as Godspeed.
succeed.g: To follow something in sequence or time.

success.e: Borrowed from Latin successus, from succēdō (“succeed”), from sub- (“next to”) + cēdō (“go, move”).
success.g: The achievement of one's aim or goal.

successful.g: Resulting in success; assuring or promoting success; accomplishing what was proposed; having the desired effect.

succession.e: From Middle English, from Old French succession, from Latin successiō (noun).
succession.g: An act, process, or instance of succeeding:

successive.g: Coming one after the other in a series.

successor.e: From Anglo-Norman successour, from Latin successor.
successor.g: A person or thing that immediately follows another in holding an office or title.

such.e: From Middle English such, swuch, swich, swilch, swulch, from Old English swelċ, from Proto-West Germanic *swalīk, from Proto-Germanic *swalīkaz (“so formed, so like”), equivalent to so + like.
such.g: Like this, that, these, those; used to make a comparison with something implied by context.

suck.e: From Middle English souken, suken, from Old English sūcan (“to suck”), from Proto-West Germanic *sūkan, from Proto-Germanic *sūkaną (“to suck, suckle”), from Proto-Indo-European *sewg-, *sewk- (“to suck”).
suck.g: An instance of drawing something into one's lungs by inhaling or into one's mouth by suction.

sudden.e: From Middle English sodeyn, sodain, from Anglo-Norman sodein, from Old French sodain, subdain (“immediate, sudden”), from Vulgar Latin *subitānus (“sudden”), from Latin subitāneus (“sudden”), from subitus (“sudden", literally, "that which has come stealthily”), originally the past participle of subīre (“to come or go stealthily”).
sudden.g: Occurring quickly with little or no warning or expectation; instantly.

suddenly.e: From Middle English sodenly, sodeynly, sodeinliche, sodaynlyche; equivalent to sudden + -ly.
suddenly.g: Happening quickly and with little or no warning; in a sudden manner.

sue.e: From Middle English seuen, sewen, siwen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman suer, siwer et al. and Old French sivre (“to follow after”) (modern French suivre), from Vulgar Latin *sequere (“to follow”), from Latin sequi.
sue.g: To file a legal action against someone, generally a non-criminal (civil) action.

suffer.e: From Middle English suffren, from Anglo-Norman suffrir, from Latin sufferre (“to offer, hold up, bear, suffer”), from sub- (“up, under”) + ferō (“to carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”).

suffering.e: By surface analysis, suffer + -ing. Mostly displaced English bale (“suffering, woe, torment”) and English woe.

suffice.e: From Middle English suffisen, from Middle French souffire, from Latin sufficiō (“supply, be adequate”), from sub (“under”) + faciō (“do, make”).
suffice.g: To be enough or sufficient; to meet the need (of anything); to be adequate; to be good enough.

sufficient.e: From Old French sufisanz, soficient, from Latin sufficiēns, present participle of sufficiō.

suggest.e: Coined based on Latin suggestus, perfect passive participle of suggerō (“bring up, bring under, lay beneath, furnish, supply, excite, advise, suggest”, verb), from sub (“from below, under”) + gerō (“bear, carry”, verb).
suggest.g: To imply but stop short of explicitly stating (something).

suggestion.e: From Middle English suggestion, from Anglo-Norman suggestioun, sugestiun, from Latin suggestiō, from suggerō (“suggest”, verb), from Latin sub- (“from below, up”) + gerō (“to bring”). Equivalent to suggest + -ion.
suggestion.g: Something suggested (with subsequent adposition being for)

suit.e: From Middle English sute, borrowed from Anglo-Norman suite, from metathesis of earlier Old French siute, from Vulgar Latin *sequita, from *sequere, from sequor, sequi, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sékʷetor, from *sekʷ-.
suit.g: A set of clothes to be worn together, now especially a man's matching jacket and trousers (also business suit or lounge suit), or a similar

sulfur.e: From Middle English sulphur, borrowed from Anglo-Norman sulfre, from Latin sulfur, from sulpur itself of uncertain origin.
sulfur.g: A chemical element with atomic number 16, having a bright yellow color and characteristic smell, used commercially in a variety of products

sullen.e: From Middle English soleyn, from Anglo-Norman soleyn (“alone”), from Old French sole (“single, sole, alone”), from Latin sōlus (“by oneself alone”). The change in meaning from "single" to morose occurred in Middle English.
sullen.g: Having a brooding ill temper; sulky.

sullied.e: From sully + -ied (suffix forming participial adjectives and past participal forms of verbs ending in -y).

sum.e: From Middle English summe, from Old French summe, from Latin summa (“highest point; sum”), from summus (“highest”).
sum.g: A quantity obtained by addition or aggregation.

sum.e: Borrowed from Kazakh сом (som), Kyrgyz сом (som), Uyghur سوم (som), and Uzbek soʻm, all of which have the core signification “pure”, used in elliptical reference to historical coins of pure gold.
sum.g: The basic unit of money in Kyrgyzstan.

summary.e: From Middle English summary, from Medieval Latin summārius, from Latin summa (“total, sum”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives).
summary.g: Concise, brief, or presented in a condensed form; presenting information in such a form.

summary.e: From Medieval Latin summārium, from Latin summa (“total, sum”) + -ārium (suffix forming nouns of purpose).
summary.g: An abstract or a condensed presentation of the substance of a body of material.

summer.e: From Middle English somer, sumer, from Old English sumor m, from Proto-West Germanic *sumar m, from Proto-Germanic *sumaraz m, derived from Proto-Indo-European *semh₂- (“summer”).
summer.g: One of four seasons, traditionally the second, marked by the longest and typically hottest days of the year due to the inclination of the Ea

summer.e: From Middle English somer, from Anglo-Norman summer, sumer, from Vulgar Latin saumārius, for Late Latin sagmārius, from Latin sagma (“sum”).
summer.g: A horizontal beam supporting a building.

summit.e: PIE word upó The noun is derived from Late Middle English somet, somete (“head, top”), from Anglo-Norman sumet and Middle French sommet (masculine), somete, sommette (“top of a thing; highest point of a mountain”) (feminine) (modern French sommet), from Old French somet, sommette.
summit.g: The topmost point or surface of a thing; the apex, the peak.

summon.e: From Anglo-Norman somoundre, from Old French sumundre, from Latin summonēre, itself from sub + monēre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *monéyeti, causative from *men- (“to think”).
summon.g: To call people together; to convene; to convoke.

summon.e: Borrowed from Malay saman (“fine, financial penalty”), which is itself borrowed from English summons (“notice summoning someone to appear in court”). This sense re-emerged in English as summon likely due to the erroneous belief that the original singular English word summons is plural.
summon.g: A fine; a fee or monetary penalty incurred for breaking the law; usually for a minor offence such as a traffic violation.

summons.e: From Middle English somouns (“order or command to do something”), borrowed from Old French sumunce (modern French semonce), from Vulgar Latin *summonsa, a noun use of the feminine past participle of summoneō, summonēre (“to summon”).
summons.g: A call to do something, especially to come.

sumptuous.e: From Middle French sumptueux, from Latin sumptuōsus, from sūmptus (“cost, charge, expense”), from sumō (“to take”) + -tus (noun formation suffix).

sun.e: From Middle English soen, son, sone, sonne, sun, sune, sunna, sunne, sunnæ, synne, zonne, zunne, from Old English sunna, sunne, sunnu (“sun”), from Proto-West Germanic *sunnā, from Proto-Germanic *sunnǭ (“sun”), from heteroclitic inanimate Proto-Indo-European *sh₂wen-, oblique of Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ (“sun”).
sun.g: A star, especially when seen as the centre of any single solar system.
A traditional Japanese unit of length, approximately 30.3 millimetres (1.193 inches).

sunder.e: From Middle English sunder, from Old English sundor- (“separate, different”), from Proto-Germanic *sundraz (“isolated, particular, alone”), from Proto-Indo-European *snter-, *seni-, *senu-, *san- (“apart, without, for oneself”).

From Middle English sundren (“to separate, part, divide”), from Old English sundrian (“to separate, split, part, divide”), from Proto-Germanic *sundrōną (“to separate”), from Proto-Indo-European *sen(e)- (“separate, without”).
sunder.g: To break or separate or to break apart, especially with force.

sundry.e: The English word is analysable as sunder + -y. The noun and pronoun are derived from the adjective.
sundry.g: More than one or two but not very many; a number of, several.

sundry.e: From Middle English sondri, sondry, syndri (“individually; now and then, occasionally; physically apart, separately; variously”), from Old English syndrige, from Old English syndriġ (adjective): see further at etymology 1.
sundry.g: Synonym of asunder (“into separate parts or pieces”).

sunlight.e: From Middle English sonnelight, sunneliht, from Old English sunnan lēoht (“sunlight”), equivalent to sun + light.
sunlight.g: All the electromagnetic radiation given off by the Sun; especially, that in the visible spectrum and that bathes the Earth.

sunrise.e: From Middle English sonne-rys, sunne ryse, equivalent to sun + rise.
sunrise.g: The time of day when the sun appears above the eastern horizon.

sunset.e: From Middle English son-sett, Sonne set, equivalent to sun + set. In Gower's Confessio Amantis, before 1393.
sunset.g: The moment each evening when the sun disappears below the western horizon.

sunshine.e: In the Coverdale Bible in 1535, in Genesis and Exodus about 1250 as Middle English sunnesine; synchronically sun + shine.
sunshine.g: The direct rays, light or warmth of the sun.

sup.e: There is no evidence of continuity with Old English supa.
sup.g: To sip; to take a small amount of food or drink into the mouth, especially with a spoon.

sup.e: From Middle English soupen, suppen, Anglo-Norman super, from supe, soupe.

superfluity.e: From superflu(ous) + -ity, Old French superfluite, from Medieval Latin superfluitas, from Latin superfluus.
superfluity.g: The quality or state of being superfluous; overflowingness.

superfluous.e: From Middle English superfluous, from Latin superfluus (“superfluous”) + -ous, from superfluō (“overflow”), from super (“above, more than, over”) + fluō (“flow”). Literally corresponds to overflow, which is from Germanic, rather than Latin.
superfluous.g: In excess of what is required or sufficient.

superior.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French superiour, from Latin superior (“higher, upper”).
superior.g: Higher in rank, status, or quality.

superscription.e: From Middle French superscription, or its source, Late Latin superscriptio, from superscribere.
superscription.g: Something written (or engraved) on the surface, outside, or above something else; specifically, an address on a letter, envelope, etc.

superstition.e: From Middle French superstition, from Latin superstitio (“superstition”), from superstāre (“to stand above, to stand upon, to survive”) + -tiō (“-tion: forming nouns”), from super- (“above, over, upon”) + stāre (“to stand”).
superstition.g: A belief considered to be irrational, unfounded, or based solely on fear and ignorance, particularly credulous reverence towards and belief

superstitious.e: From Old French superstitieux, from Latin superstitiōsus, from superstitio + -ōsus.

supervise.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin supervisus, from supervidere, from Latin super + videre.
supervise.g: To oversee or direct (a task or organization).

supervisor.g: A person with the official task of overseeing the work of a person or group, or of other operations and activities.

supper.e: From Middle English soper, from Old French soper, from sope (“soup”).
supper.g: An optional light meal consumed shortly before going to bed.

supplant.e: From Middle English supplanten, supplaunten, from Old French supplanter, from Latin supplantō (“trip up”), from sub (“from below, under”) + planta (“sole”).
supplant.g: To take the place of; to replace, to supersede.

supple.e: From Middle English souple, from Old French souple, soupple (“soft, lithe, yielding”), from Latin supplic-, supplex (“suppliant, submissive, kneeling”), of uncertain formation. Either from sub + plicō (“bend”) (compare complex), or from sub + plācō (“placate”).

suppliant.e: From French suppliant, present participle of supplier.

supplication.e: From Middle English supplicacioun, supplication, from Old French supplication, from Latin supplicatio, supplicationem, from supplicare (“to supplicate”). By surface analysis, supplicate + -ion.
supplication.g: An act of supplicating; a humble request.

supply.e: From Middle English supplien, borrowed from Old French soupleer, souploier, from Latin suppleo (“to fill up, make full, complete, supply”). The Middle English spelling was modified to conform to Latin etymology.
supply.g: To provide (something), to make (something) available for use.
Supplely: in a supple manner, with suppleness.

support.e: From Middle English supporten, from Old French supporter, from Latin supportō.
From Middle English support, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French support.

suppose.e: From Middle English supposen, borrowed from Old French supposer, equivalent to prefix sub- (“under”) + poser (“to place”); corresponding in meaning to Latin supponere (“to put under, to substitute, falsify, counterfeit”), suppositum.
suppose.g: To take for granted; to conclude, with less than absolute supporting data; to believe.

suppress.e: From Latin suppressus, perfect passive participle of supprimō (“press down or under”), from sub (“under”) + premō (“press”).
suppress.g: To put an end to, especially with force, to crush, do away with; to prohibit, subdue.

supreme.e: From Middle English suppreme, partly from Middle French suppreme, supreme and partly from its etymon, Latin suprēmus, superlative of superus (“that is above”). In the cooking sense, partly an independent borrowing of French suprême, partly merged with the existing English word.
supreme.g: Dominant, having power over all others.

sure.e: From Middle English sure, seur, sur, from Middle French sur or Old French seür, from Latin sēcūrus (“secure”, literally “carefree”), from sē- (“apart”) + cūra (“care”) (compare Old English orsorg (“carefree”), from or- (“without”) + sorg (“care”)).
sure.g: Physically secure and certain, non-failing, reliable.

surely.e: From Middle English surely; equivalent to sure + -ly.

surety.e: From Middle English surete, attested since the early 1300s in the sense "guarantee, promise, pledge, assurance", from Anglo-Norman seurté/Old French seurté with the same meaning (whence modern French sûreté), from Latin sēcūritās. Equivalent to sure + -ty. The senses "security, safety, stability" and "certainty" are attested since the late 1300s.

surface.e: Borrowed from Middle French surface. By surface analysis, sur- + face.
surface.g: The external boundary of an object or body.

surfeit.e: From Middle English surfeite, surfet, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman surfet, surfeit and Old French sorfet, sorfait, past participle of surfaire (“to augment, exaggerate, exceed”), from sur- (“over”) + faire (“to do”).

surge.e: From Middle English sourge, of uncertain origin. In the earliest examples, translating Old French sourgeon (modern French surgeon), from sourge- (which the Middle English term is probably from), the present stem of sourdre, from Latin surgō (“to rise”).

surname.e: From Middle English surname, a partial calque of Old French surnum, surnoun (“surname; nickname”) (whence Middle English surnoun), from Late Latin supernōmen, suprānōmen (“surname”), from super- (“over, above, beyond”) and nōmen (“name”), equivalent to sur- + name.
surname.g: The portion of a person's name that is generally hereditary or treated as an indicator of a person's family, which may be shared with other

surpass.e: From Middle French surpasser (“to pass beyond”). By surface analysis, sur- + pass.
surpass.g: To go beyond or exceed (something) in an adjudicative or literal sense.

surplus.e: From Middle English surplus, from Middle French surplus.
surplus.g: That which remains when use or need is satisfied, or when a limit is reached; excess; overplus; overage.

surprise.e: From Middle English surprise, borrowed from Middle French surprise (“an overtake”), nominal use of the past participle of Old French sorprendre (“to overtake”), from sor- (“over”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin super- + Latin prendere, contracted from prehendere (“to grasp, seize”).

surrender.e: From Middle English surrendren, from Old French surrendre, from sur- + rendre (“render”).
surrender.g: To give up into the power, control, or possession of another.

surrender.e: From Middle English surrendre, from Anglo-Norman surrendre, infinitive as noun.
surrender.g: An act of surrendering, submission into the possession of another; a feeling of abandonment and resignation; the deliberate cessation of str

surround.e: From Middle English sourrounden (“to submerge, overflow”), from Middle French souronder, suronder, from Late Latin superundō, from super + undō (“to rise in waves”), from unda (“wave”).
surround.g: To encircle something or simultaneously extend in all directions.

survey.e: From Middle English surveyen, from Old French sourveoir, surveer (“to oversee”), from sour-, sur- (“over”) + veoir, veeir (“to see”), from Latin videre.
survey.g: The act of surveying; a general view.

survive.e: From Anglo-Norman survivre, Old French survivre, from Late Latin supervīvere (“to outlive”), from Latin super (“over”) + vivere (“to live”), akin to vita (“life”).
survive.g: To continue to live; to remain alive.

suspect.e: From Old French suspect, from Latin suspectus, perfect passive participle of suspiciō (“mistrust, suspect”), from sub (“under”), + speciō (“watch, look at”).
suspect.g: To imagine or suppose (something) to be true, or to exist, without proof.

suspend.e: From Old French sospendre, from Latin suspendere.

suspense.e: From Middle English suspense, suspence, from Anglo-Norman suspens (as in en suspens) and Old French suspens, from Latin suspēnsus.
suspense.g: The condition of being suspended; cessation for a time.

suspicion.e: From Middle English suspecioun, borrowed from Latin suspīciō, suspīciōnem, from suspicere, from sub- (“up to”) with specere (“to look at”). Perhaps partly through the influence of Old French sospeçon (or rather the Anglo-Norman form suspecioun). Equivalent to suspect + -ion.
suspicion.g: The act of suspecting something or someone, especially of something wrong.

sustain.e: From Middle English susteinen, sustenen, from Old French sustenir (French soutenir), from Latin sustineō, sustinēre (“to uphold”), from sub- (“from below, up”) + teneō (“hold”, verb).
sustain.g: To maintain, or keep in existence.

sustenance.e: From Middle English sustenaunce, from Old French sustenance, from sustenir with the suffix -ance, from Vulgar Latin *sustenire, from Latin sustinere. Equivalent to sustain + -ance.
sustenance.g: Something that provides support or nourishment.

sing.e: From Middle English syngen, from Old English singan (“to sing”), from Proto-West Germanic *singwan, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną (“to sing”), from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ- (“to recite, sing”).
sing.g: To produce musical or harmonious sounds with one’s voice.

sink.e: From Middle English synken, from Old English sincan, from Proto-West Germanic *sinkwan, from Proto-Germanic *sinkwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷ- (“to fall, sink”). In the causative sense, it replaced Old English senċan (“make sink”) from Proto-Germanic *sankwijaną.
sink.g: To move or be moved into something.
